passages.happening:
“Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God. And that is what we are! The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know Him” (verse 1).

“Beloved, we are now children of God, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is. And everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure” (verses 2-3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 2 ended with being ‘born of Him’. Now John stops to wonder at it. ‘Behold what manner of love.’ The words carry surprise: what kind of love is this, from what country does it come? The Father has called us his children. And then, so that no one thinks it is only a polite name, John adds, ‘And that is what we are’.

In the ancient world a father gave a child his name, his place, his inheritance and his likeness. Children were expected to resemble their father and to honour him. To be called God's children is to be given all of that.

Then John looks both ways in time. ‘We are now children of God.’ That is already true, on good days and bad. But ‘what we will be has not yet been revealed’. There is more to come. When Christ appears, ‘we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is’. Seeing him will change us.

And that hope works backward into the present. ‘Everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself.’ People who know where they are going begin to live like it now.

Notice one small detail. In his letters John calls believers God's ‘children’, and keeps the word ‘Son’ for Jesus. Believers are God's children by new birth. Jesus is the Son in a way no one else is.
passages.ot:
The wonder of being God's children reaches back to Israel: “You are sons of the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 14:1). And the prophets saw God's love as a father's: “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son” (Hosea 11:1).

The hope of seeing God is the psalm's: “As for me, I will behold Your face in righteousness; when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence” (Psalm 17:15).
passages.asks: Ask whether you believe that you are, now, a child of God, even on a bad day. Ask what it would mean to live today in the light of what you will one day be. And ask whom you could remind of the Father's love.

passages.happening:
“Everyone who practices sin practices lawlessness as well. Indeed, sin is lawlessness. But you know that Christ appeared to take away sins, and in Him there is no sin. No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning. No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him” (verses 4-6).

“Little children, let no one deceive you: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous. The one who practices sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the very start. This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil” (verses 7-8).

“Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin, because God’s seed abides in him; he cannot go on sinning, because he has been born of God. By this the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil: Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone who does not love his brother” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
‘Let no one deceive you.’ Someone was teaching that a person could be righteous without doing what is right, perhaps that spiritual knowledge lifted a person above moral concern. Later Christian writers describe groups who held either that the body did not matter and could be indulged, or that the truly spiritual were beyond sin. It is wise not to read those later systems back into this letter. But John is plainly answering something like them.

He begins with what sin is. ‘Sin is lawlessness.’ The word is anomia. It is not only breaking a rule. It is refusing God's rightful rule. The same word was used for the rebellion expected in the last days. To call all sin lawlessness is to show which side it takes.

Then he shows why sin and Christ cannot be friends. Christ ‘appeared to take away sins’, and ‘in Him there is no sin’. He was ‘revealed, to destroy the works of the devil’. A life that settles into sin goes against everything he came to do.

And then the strong words. ‘No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning.’ ‘Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin, because God’s seed abides in him.’ The seed is God's own life planted in the believer. Readers have taken it as that new life, as the Holy Spirit, or as God's word. On any reading, it is God's life in a person that will not let him make his home in sin.

Verse 10 joins the two marks the letter keeps returning to: doing what is right, and loving one's brother.
passages.ot:
The serpent's lie in Eden lies behind ‘the devil has been sinning from the very start’: “You will not surely die,” the serpent told the woman (Genesis 3:4). And the first promise of victory over him came then too: “He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel” (Genesis 3:15).

The prophets promised a new heart that would walk in God's ways: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” and “cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:26-27).

And the psalm prays for a clean heart from God himself: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10).
passages.hard:
How can John say that no one born of God keeps on sinning, when in chapter 1 he said that anyone who claims to have no sin is deceived?

This is one of the best-known puzzles in the letter, and Christians have read it in several ways. These notes do not choose.

Many point to the Greek verbs in chapter 3, which often describe ongoing action. On this reading John means that a child of God does not keep on sinning as a settled way of life, while he still commits sins that need confessing. The BSB follows this reading with ‘keeps on sinning’ and ‘refuses to practice sin’.

Others think grammar alone cannot carry the weight. They read John as speaking of a particular kind of sin: the deliberate rejection of God shown by those who left, or sin as ‘lawlessness’, a settled refusal of God's rule.

Others read John as describing what the new birth produces in principle and what a Christian is becoming, set against teachers who said that sin did not matter.

And the Wesleyan tradition has drawn on these verses in teaching that believers can be freed from willful sin.

None of these readings says that a true Christian never sins. John has already said, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1:8), and he wrote chapter 2 for those who do sin: they have an advocate with the Father. Across the readings the balance is John's own. Do not deny your sin, and do not make peace with it.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whether there is a sin you have made peace with, and treated as just the way you are. Ask what it means to you that Christ came to destroy the works of the devil, including the ones in your own life. And if you struggle and fall, ask whether you are running to your advocate or away from him.

passages.happening:
“This is the message you have heard from the beginning: We should love one another. Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did Cain slay him? Because his own deeds were evil, while those of his brother were righteous” (verses 11-12).

“So do not be surprised, brothers, if the world hates you. We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers. The one who does not love remains in death. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that eternal life does not reside in a murderer” (verses 13-15).
passages.hearers:
John turns from righteousness to love, and he begins with the oldest story of a brother's hatred. Cain is the only Old Testament figure John names in this letter. By the first century Jewish teachers already used Cain as the pattern of envy and hatred. John says why Cain killed: not because Abel had wronged him, but because Abel's deeds were right and his own were evil. Goodness can provoke hatred in those who do not want to change.

So John's readers should not be surprised if the world hates them. The good can be hated simply for being good.

Then John gives a sign of new life: ‘we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers.’ Love does not earn the new life. It shows that it has come.

And then a hard sentence. ‘Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.’ John is following Jesus, who said that anger against a brother is already under judgment (Matthew 5:21-22). Hatred is murder in the heart, the seed from which Cain's act grew. John does not mean that feeling hurt or angry makes a person a killer. He means that settled hatred, wishing a brother gone, belongs to death, not life.
passages.ot:
Cain's story is in Genesis. God warned him first: “sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it” (Genesis 4:7). Then “Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him” (Genesis 4:8).

The law forbade hatred inside the heart, not only the deed: “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart” (Leviticus 19:17).

And the proverb sets love and hatred side by side: “Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions” (Proverbs 10:12).
passages.hard:
‘Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.’ What if I have strong feelings of anger toward someone who hurt me? Am I a murderer?

No. Anger at a real wrong is not the same as the settled hatred John means. The Bible itself says, “Be angry, yet do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). Many psalms pour out anger to God about people who did harm. John is speaking of a heart that wishes a brother gone and nurses that wish, the kind of heart that grew into Cain's act.

If you have been badly hurt, these verses do not tell you to pretend it did not happen or to stay close to someone who is harming you. They tell you not to let hatred make its home in you, and to bring your anger to God.

Where a crime has been done, it is right to report it to the authorities. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whether there is someone whose goodness irritates you, and why. Ask whether you are nursing a grudge that wishes someone gone. And ask what passing ‘from death to life’ looks like in the way you treat the people closest to you.

passages.happening: “By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers. If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him? Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth” (verses 16-18).
passages.hearers:
Here John gives the letter's clearest definition of love. ‘By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us.’ Love is not first a feeling. It is learned by looking at the cross.

And because Jesus laid down his life, ‘we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers’. John then brings it down to an ordinary day. Laying down your life will not usually mean dying. It will often mean opening your purse. ‘If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion.’ In the Roman world there was no public welfare. Famine and debt could ruin a family quickly. Early Christian churches became known for caring for their own poor and their widows.

The word for compassion is, in Greek, the inner organs, which ancient people thought of as the seat of feeling. To close your heart is, literally, to shut up your insides against your brother. John asks: how can the love of God live in someone like that?

His last line is plain: love ‘not in word and speech, but in action and truth’. Kind words that cost nothing are not what John means.
passages.ot:
The law commanded open hands toward the poor: “If there is a poor man among your brothers within any of the gates in the land that the LORD your God is giving you, then you are not to harden your heart or shut your hand from your poor brother” (Deuteronomy 15:7).

The prophets measured true worship by the same test: “Isn’t it to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home, to clothe the naked when you see him, and not to turn away from your own flesh and blood?” (Isaiah 58:7).
passages.hard:
Does ‘we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers’ mean I must stay where I am being harmed, or give until I have nothing left?

No. John's measure is Christ's love, which seeks the good of others. It does not ask anyone to stay where they are being hurt. And this verse is about love freely given, not about letting someone take from you by force or fear.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whom you know who is in need right now, and what you have that could help. Ask whether your love is mostly words, or whether it costs you something. And ask what the cross teaches you about what love is.

passages.t: God is greater than our hearts
passages.happening:
“And by this we will know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts in His presence: Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (verses 19-20).

“Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God, and we will receive from Him whatever we ask, because we keep His commandments and do what is pleasing in His sight. And this is His commandment: that we should believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ, and we should love one another just as He commanded us. Whoever keeps His commandments remains in God, and God in him. And by this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us” (verses 21-24).
passages.hearers:
After hard words about love, some readers would feel their hearts sink. Had they loved enough? John speaks straight to that. ‘Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things.’

This is one of the tenderest sentences in the letter. Our hearts can accuse us, sometimes truly and sometimes far beyond the truth. John does not say, ‘Try harder to feel better.’ He says God is greater. God knows everything, including what we cannot see in ourselves, and his judgment, not our self-accusation, is the last word.

When the heart is at peace, there is confidence in prayer. John says believers will receive what they ask, as they keep his commands and do what pleases him. This is not a magic formula. It describes children who know and love their father's will, and ask in line with it (John says so again in 5:14).

Then John puts the whole command in one sentence, and it has two parts: believe in the name of his Son, and love one another. Belief and love are not two commands but one.

The chapter ends with the Spirit. ‘By this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us.’ That leads straight into chapter 4, where John shows how to recognise the Spirit of God.
passages.ot:
The psalms know the heart that accuses, and the God who searches it: “Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my concerns” (Psalm 139:23).

And they know God's mercy is greater than our failures: “As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12). “For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14).

Confidence in prayer is the psalm's too: “The LORD is near to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth” (Psalm 145:18).
passages.hard:
What should I do when my heart keeps condemning me, even after I have confessed?

John's answer is that God is greater than your heart. Your feelings of guilt are not the final judge. God knows all things, including your faith in his Son and your love for others, however weak they seem to you. The letter's whole aim is that believers may know they have eternal life (5:13).

Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith.

If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what your heart most often accuses you of, and whether you have brought it to God. Ask whether you believe that God is greater than your heart. And ask how believing in Jesus and loving others belong together in your life this week.
